title: Shinran
hookLine: Honen's student: even good people are saved, so how much more the bad (Tannisho 3)

lines: EVEN THE GOOD ARE BORN THERE.
cards: Here is a sentence that sounds like a typo. Even a good person is born in the Pure Land. How much more, then, the bad person.
Read it again; it isn't backward by accident. The ordinary saying ran the other way: even a bad person can be saved, so surely a good one will be.

The man who flipped it was Honen's student, a monk named Shinran, and his words were remembered and written down by a disciple in a small book called the Tannisho. It is in the third section. Today, Shinran.

teach.b: First, the book. Its title speaks of lamenting differences. A disciple, traditionally named Yuien, wrote down sayings he had heard from Shinran, because after the teacher's death he saw the teaching being bent.
So these are remembered words, gathered with care. Second, the flip. In the third section, Shinran explains.

teach.h: THE GOOD STILL LEAN ON THEMSELVES.
teach.b: A good person, someone confident in their own good deeds, is still leaning partly on their own effort. They haven't wholly entrusted themselves to Amida's vow.
They can still be born in the Pure Land, he says, if they turn and entrust. Third, who the vow is for. People full of passions and confusion, he says, cannot free themselves by any practice at all.

teach.h: THE VOW WAS MADE FOR THE BAD.
teach.b: Amida made the vow out of compassion for exactly them. So the person who knows they are bad, and has nothing left to lean on but the vow, is the one it was meant for in the first place. Not an exception.
The point. Fourth, what it is not. This is not permission to do harm.

teach.h: NOT PERMISSION: AN ANTIDOTE, NOT POISON.
teach.b: Elsewhere in the same book Shinran warns against taking poison just because there is an antidote.
His teaching is about where trust rests: not in how good you've managed to be, but in Amida's compassion, which Pure Land Buddhists call Other Power.
The one who can't pretend to be good, in Shinran's eyes, is closest to the door.

how: In Jodo Shinshu, the school that grew from Shinran's teaching, people say Namu Amida Butsu as an expression of gratitude rather than as a practice to earn birth, and the Tannisho is read and discussed in study groups.

o: Honen's student who said: how much more the bad
a scribe who copied out the Tannisho for temples

still leaning on their own effort

games.q: you're Shinran's student. you hear him say, even a good person is born in the Pure Land; how much more the bad person. what does he mean?
o: being bad is better than being good
the vow was made for those who can't save themselves
games.why: Shinran taught that Amida's vow was made out of compassion for people who can't free themselves; the good can be born there too, once they entrust.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose faults you know well, someone who irritates you or lets people down; maybe it's you.
Without excusing anything or arguing the case, notice that they are struggling, as people do, and on each out-breath let a little of the judging loosen, the way you'd loosen a too-tight grip.
If it's hard, start again with something smaller.

wordCard.voice: Shinran. Honen's student, who taught that Amida's vow was made above all for those who know they can't save themselves. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese akunin shoki: the bad person is the true object of Amida's vow, the idea behind Tannisho 3.

carryVoice: Your line: how much more the bad. Trust rests on Amida's compassion, not on how good you've managed to be. Day nine hundred ninety-three, counted.
